blocks.x: The martial art of Aikido has a variety of teachings and practices within it, and within that is a great variety depending on the style of Aikido you train in, your teachers (senseis), and where you train. One comment I’ve heard on several occasions is how Aikido claims to use some “magic” force to throw people, sometimes involving people who are across the mat. Perhaps this claim is more often associated with Ki Aikido, a style that I have extensively trained and taught in.
I think this is an interesting topic because while some of these claims seem doubtable, there is a kernel of truth here. So I want to dedicate an article talking about this topic in some depth.

Before I go any further I want to make it clear that regardless of the amount of training I have, I am still a shodan (first level black belt), and compared to other people I’ve trained with, I have a small fraction of total years training. Furthermore, this is not a topic we talk about explicitly often. So please consider what I have to say more of an informed opinion instead of the official word from an aikido master (which I am not by any means).
First, I want to talk about a specific waza (technique) where I think something like “touchless” throwing occurs, and then I’ll discuss some of the more abstract types of this.

In Ki Aikido we have a waza called “Yokomen-uchi Irimi”. In short, person A attacks person B with what looks like a diagonal karate chop to the neck, and person B puts out their hands with the right timing and “Ki” in order to throw them. If executed correctly on both sides, this throw can look like there is no physical contact, and in some cases that may very well be the case.

Doing Aikido at a high level that looks “good” requires the use of a skilled “Uke” (attacker) doing “ukemi”, which is essentially the way of falling safely (and something I’ve written about before). A good Uke should attack with vigor and Ki, follow accurately when they are led, and fall in a way that is safe to both parties. But there is a line between moving as one is led, and simply throwing one’s own body in a dramatic way, something I’ll come back to in just a moment.

In the case of Yokomen-uchi Irimi, a mediocre Uke may let their arm be struck hard by the Nage (the one performing the waza) and then fall down. This can demonstrate that the Nage threw correctly, but is not ideal since doing this sort of thing over and over can cause bruising on the Uke side. That’s why a skilled Uke will endeavor to fall before they make physical contact, which means as they feel they are about to be struck, they slide their feet forward in something akin to a baseball slide. In this case, we would say the Uke felt the “Ki” of the nage, and fell at the appropriate time in response. The word “Ki” is a bit tricky to explain, but for now I’ll just say we consider it to be the energy of the universe, though sometimes “Ki” can manifest as someone’s “intention”. We don’t normally use terms like “I felt your intention”, but I think it’s a fair way to think about it, especially for those new to this martial art.

Having said that, if the Uke decides to throw him or herself and slide even though they are not feeling the Nage’s “Ki”, for the purpose of a good visual or show, it can turn into a type of acting and ruin the point of the entire exercise.

If you want to see this technique in action, check out around 0:20 in this video. While I think there might be a tiny bit of contact, this demonstrates a professional Uke who is moving very smoothly and responding to Ki.

By the way, the Ki Aikido I train in generally does not use the term “touchless”. The closest term that describe this type of throw is “sousho” (叢書), a term borrowed from calligraphy that expresses a very free stroke. Even this word isn’t used that often in my training, though I’ve heard it a few times. I don’t think it necessarily means “touchless”, but rather emphasizes throwing with more Ki and not focusing on the physical aspect.

One more “touchless” exercise we do in Ki Aikido is where two people stand facing one another, with a bit of space between, and hold up two bokken (wooden swords) facing each other’s throats. If the Nage moves forward with sufficient “Ki”, the Uke should feel that and start moving backwards to protect themselves. While this one is a bit more abstract, I think when done correctly there is no magic or acting, and this accurately reflects the concept of “Ki” that we practice. By the way, both this exercise and the previous one are somewhat advanced techniques, but I chose them since I think it illustrates the point well. These are exercises I have done many times, though I admit my Ukemi on the first is awkward, and I am not particularly good at the second.

You can take this “being thrown by Ki” to a further extent, where (based on some videos online) you see a sensei at the other side of the mat flipping a finger and having someone far away suddenly do a flip, as if thrown by magic. To be honest, this is not something I’ve ever heard of or seen in Ki Aikido, and furthermore I hesitate to speak critically about people in other styles of Aikido.
I will say that these sorts of techniques seem a bit suspicious, though until I was actually thrown by someone with such a power, I can’t speak on the truth of it.

An important part of the training is learning to be sensitive to Ki, and being able to respond as an Uke when you feel it, whether that is backing up or doing a roll, whatever. As you become more sensitive, you become more able to react to Ki on a faster time scale. But in the two Ki Aikido examples I gave above (Yokomen-uchi Irimi and Bokken training), there is a clear logic to what is happening: the uke is moving in response to feeling danger, and moving to protect themself.

If you tried to do either of these techniques with an inexperienced Uke (or a person off the street), they could get injured if they didn’t respond (though I would argue it is the Nage’s responsibility to not hurt the Uke). So in these cases I think the technique could still “work” to a certain extent even if the Uke doesn’t know anything about Ki Aikido, which to me shows there is some truth involved, and it’s not all just an act for show.
Can a sensei send enough “Ki” to an Uke on the other side of the mat to make them seriously feel imminent danger? Or is it just an act of taking things too far, beyond any real-world application?

I want to take a step back and say something here that I feel is important. Whether throwing with Ki at a far distance is real or not, I don’t think it should be the purpose of anyone’s training. A trainee should buy into, and at least partially understand, the principles, philosophies, and other key elements of any martial art. Ultimately I feel that Aikido (and probably many other martial arts) are more about self development than self defense, though that is surely an undertone of the latter more or less (depending on the style). I could imagine someone trying to dedicate their life to meeting senseis around the world to find one that could throw him or her from afar with Ki, but I think that would be a waste of time.

I will also say that based on all the stuff I’ve learned in Ki Aikido so far, even if I could throw someone across the room with Ki, I don’t think I would ever want or need to do it. A simpler, more realistic example of this is someone who exudes positivity and is brimming with charisma. Such a person can be said to be extending “Ki” and may influence those around him or her in a positive way.

To put it another way: a criminal begins to approach an old man in a dark alleyway, but once the criminal gets closer he sees the old man has a certain energy about him, a certain positivity, and the old man even seems to be smiling to himself as he adeptly navigates the water-filled potholes at his feet without stumbling. The criminal realizes that attacking the old man is probably a bad idea and wouldn’t go well anyway, and turns away.

While the old man didn’t “throw” the criminal with Ki, his Ki exerted an influence upon the criminal that changed what might have happened. This is a good real-world example I can give of using Ki to influence another.
